title: Is the God of the Old Testament the God of Jesus?
excerpt: In the second century a Christian named Marcion decided the God of Israel could not be the Father of Jesus and cut the Old Testament out of his Bible. The church refused him and kept the harder book, with its flood, its wars and its mercy, and the question he asked has not gone away.
body:
A woman set out in January to read the whole Bible in a year. She got through Genesis and Exodus, slowed down in Leviticus, and stopped in the book of Joshua some time in March, after Jericho, and she hasn't picked the plan up again. A father reading a picture book about Noah was asked by his five-year-old what happened to the other children, and he changed the subject. A student says he has no quarrel with Jesus. It's the Father he can't stand.

The skeptic puts it more sharply than any of them. The first three quarters of the Christian Bible, he says, describe a god who drowns the world, kills the firstborn of Egypt and orders cities emptied of everything that breathes. The last quarter describes a teacher who tells people to love their enemies. Either these are two different gods, or one god changed his character somewhere between Malachi and Matthew, and Christians should say which.

The objection is old, and it was first made inside the church by a Christian. He believed he was defending Jesus.

## The First Man to Solve It

His name was Marcion. He came from Pontus, on the south shore of the Black Sea, and he taught in Rome around the year 140, in the reign of the emperor Antoninus. His own book, the *Antitheses*, is lost, and what is known of it comes from the men who wrote against him, which is a reason for some caution.

Irenaeus, a bishop writing a generation later, says that Marcion built on an earlier teacher in Rome named Cerdo, who held that the God of the law and the prophets was not the Father of Jesus Christ. In Irenaeus's report Marcion declared the God of Israel "to be the author of evils, to take delight in war, to be infirm of purpose, and even to be contrary to Himself." Jesus, he taught, had come from a different and higher God. Tertullian, the North African who wrote five books against him around the year 200, summed up the two gods in a sentence: one "judicial, harsh, mighty in war; the other mild, placid," and good without qualification.

Marcion then did the consistent thing. He threw out the Scriptures of Israel altogether. Of the Christian writings he kept one Gospel, Luke's, and a collection of Paul's letters, and he edited those. Irenaeus says he removed from Luke what was written about the Lord's birth and much of the teaching in which Jesus speaks of the Maker of the world as his Father, and that he "dismembered the Epistles of Paul" in the same way.

His case should be heard at its strength, because he wasn't a fool and his churches outlasted him by generations. He had read the same pages the woman with the reading plan has read. He saw that the law says an eye for an eye and that Jesus says to turn the other cheek. Tertullian reports that he began from a saying of Jesus himself, that a good tree does not bear bad fruit. If the fruit is a drowned world and a burned city, Marcion reasoned, the tree is not the Father of Jesus. His answer was simple, and it let a Christian love Jesus without having to answer for Joshua.

The site's church history lists his teaching among [the heresies](/theology/history#heresies) the early church answered, and its entry says the idea returns "whenever people set a gentle Jesus against an embarrassing Old Testament and quietly drop the parts of the Bible they find hard."

## Why the Church Refused

The church said no, and the refusal cost something. Marcion's Bible was easier to defend than the one the church kept.

The first reason was Jesus. The only Bible Jesus had was the one Marcion threw away. When he was asked for the greatest commandment he quoted Deuteronomy, "Hear, O Israel: The Lord our God, the Lord is one" (Mark 12:29), and for the second he quoted Leviticus, "You shall love your neighbor as yourself" (Mark 12:31). When he argued about the resurrection he appealed to the burning bush and to the one who said, "I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob" (Mark 12:26). He told a crowd on a hillside, "Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets; I have not come to abolish them but to fulfill them" (Matthew 5:17). A Jesus who came from some other god could only be had by cutting sentences out of the Gospels, and Irenaeus noticed that Marcion had done exactly that. He was furnishing his disciples, Irenaeus wrote, "not with the Gospel, but merely a fragment of it."

The second reason was an argument about goodness, and Tertullian made it. Marcion wanted a God who was only kind and never judged. Tertullian answered that such a God would not be good. "For nothing is good which is unjust," he wrote. A God who watched the strong devour the weak and never once called it to account would be indifferent, and few victims of a real crime have mistaken indifference for love. Mercy and justice, on this argument, both come from the one God's care for what he has made.

The third reason was the faith the churches had been baptizing people into from the start. Irenaeus put it in a sentence: "there is one and the same God the Father, who was declared by the prophets, but made manifest by Christ." The creeds open on the same note. Before they say anything about Jesus they confess one God, the Father almighty, maker of heaven and earth. The site's page on the Apostles' Creed notes that the line was aimed at Marcion and teachers like him. It says that the one who made the world is the one who came to save it.

The men who answered Marcion did not always answer him well. Tertullian opens his first book with a page of insults about the weather of Pontus and the savagery of its people before he reaches an argument. A serious question was met with contempt as well as reasons, and we have often done the same since.

## The Charge at Full Strength

Refusing Marcion's answer does nothing to remove his question, and it should be stated without softening.

Of the flood, Genesis says that "everything on the dry land in whose nostrils was the breath of life died" (Genesis 7:22). On the night of the exodus, "the Lord struck down all the firstborn in the land of Egypt, from the firstborn of Pharaoh who sat on his throne to the firstborn of the captive who was in the dungeon" (Exodus 12:29). The captive in the dungeon had not enslaved anybody. For the cities of Canaan the instruction was "you shall save alive nothing that breathes" (Deuteronomy 20:16). The order against Amalek names "child and infant" (1 Samuel 15:3).

A reader who is troubled by these pages has read them correctly. She has also been taught to be troubled by the same book. It is the Old Testament that says, "The son shall not suffer for the iniquity of the father" (Ezekiel 18:20).

On the wars of Canaan this site already has three pages, and this essay agrees with them and will not go over their ground. The essay [Did God Command Genocide?](/writing/did-god-command-genocide) and the longer treatment of [the command to destroy the Canaanites](/questions/old-testament/the-command-to-destroy-the-canaanites) set out the several ways Christians who receive these books as Scripture read those commands, with what each reading costs. The second of them says that under every reading two things hold: "the command was tied to one land and one moment, and it gives no one today any warrant for violence." A third page argues the question of [the God of the Old Testament](/questions/old-testament/the-god-of-the-old-testament) step by step. None of them claims the difficulty is gone.

## Mercy Before the Gospels

What Marcion's picture leaves out is most of the Old Testament.

When God tells Moses his own name, after Israel has made the golden calf, this is what he says about himself: "The Lord, the Lord, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness, keeping steadfast love for thousands, forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin, but who will by no means clear the guilty" (Exodus 34:6-7). Mercy comes first in the sentence and gets the larger number. The steadfast love runs to thousands and the visiting of iniquity to "the third and the fourth generation." The Study Bible's note on [Exodus 34](/study/bible/exodus/34) observes that these phrases "reappear more than any other description of God in the Old Testament."

One prophet quotes them as a complaint. Jonah was sent to Nineveh, the great city of Assyria, the empire that would destroy his country, and he ran the other way. When the city repented and God spared it, he said why he had run: "I knew that you are a gracious God and merciful, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love, and relenting from disaster" (Jonah 4:2). The Old Testament contains a prophet who is angry at God for being too kind to foreigners.

The flood story itself does not read the way the charge assumes. Before the rain, "the Lord regretted that he had made man on the earth, and it grieved him to his heart" (Genesis 6:6). Afterward God binds himself by a promise: "never again shall there be a flood to destroy the earth" (Genesis 9:11). The story does not show a God who enjoys what he does.

The prophets who speak most about God's anger also speak about what it costs him. "How can I give you up, O Ephraim? How can I hand you over, O Israel?" God says through Hosea. "My heart recoils within me; my compassion grows warm and tender" (Hosea 11:8). Ezekiel was told to say, "I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live" (Ezekiel 33:11).

Much of the anger is anger on someone's behalf. The law that frightens modern readers is also the law that says of the widow and the orphan, "if you do mistreat them, and they cry out to me, I will surely hear their cry, and my wrath will burn" (Exodus 22:23-24). It is the law that commands, of the foreigner living in the land, "you shall love him as yourself, for you were strangers in the land of Egypt" (Leviticus 19:34). And there is a story in the books of the Kings in which a prophet has an enemy army at his mercy and tells the king of Israel, "Set bread and water before them, that they may eat and drink and go to their master" (2 Kings 6:22). The king gave them a feast and sent them home.

The Jewish people have read these Scriptures for longer than the church has existed, and have not read them as the record of a cruel god. When Christians speak of "the Old Testament God" as harsh and their own as kind, they repeat Marcion's error and insult their neighbors in the same breath. The essay on [the church and antisemitism](/writing/is-the-church-responsible-for-antisemitism) tells where that habit led.

## Judgment on the Lips of Jesus

The other half of Marcion's picture fails as well. The Jesus of the Gospels is not mild in the way it requires.

He told his own disciples, "do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul. Rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in hell" (Matthew 10:28). When people brought him news of a massacre, he did not comfort them. He said, "unless you repent, you will all likewise perish" (Luke 13:3). He told the towns that had watched his miracles and shrugged that "it will be more tolerable on the day of judgment for the land of Sodom than for you" (Matthew 11:24). He treated the flood as a thing that happened and a warning of what is coming: "the flood came and destroyed them all" (Luke 17:27). His parable of the sheep and the goats ends with the words "these will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life" (Matthew 25:46).

The rest of the New Testament follows him. The letter to the Hebrews says, "It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God" (Hebrews 10:31), and it quotes Deuteronomy to say why: "our God is a consuming fire" (Hebrews 12:29). The last book of the Bible speaks of "the wrath of the Lamb" (Revelation 6:16).

So the objection cuts both ways. The flood ends with a rainbow and a promise, and the judgment Jesus warns of comes with no such ending. Anyone who rejects the God of Noah for his severity will have to reject a good deal of Jesus on the same ground, as Marcion found when he had to edit the only Gospel he kept. The essays here on hell, among them [whether it is fair](/writing/is-hell-real-and-is-it-fair), take up that harder subject and the ways Christians understand it.

## What Changed

None of this means that nothing changed between the Testaments. "Long ago, at many times and in many ways, God spoke to our fathers by the prophets, but in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son" (Hebrews 1:1-2).

Some changes are plain. The New Testament contains no command to fight for God. When a Samaritan village would not receive Jesus, James and John offered to call down fire from heaven, as a prophet once had, and Luke says only that "he turned and rebuked them" (Luke 9:55). The people of God stopped being a nation with borders and an army and became a church scattered through every nation, and the weapons of Joshua were never handed to it.

How to describe that movement is argued among Christians. Some speak of promise and fulfillment, some of a revelation that unfolds by stages, and some of a God who stooped to the understanding of an ancient world and must be read through Christ. This essay doesn't choose among them. What they share is the thing the church held against Marcion. The speaker in the two Testaments is the same God, and what Jesus brought was more light on him. Jesus said so himself when a disciple asked to be shown the Father: "Whoever has seen me has seen the Father" (John 14:9).

Christians also confess that the two halves of the sentence spoken to Moses meet in one place. A God who forgives iniquity and a God who will not clear the guilty look like a contradiction until the cross, where, Paul says, God acted "so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus" (Romans 3:26). The judgment the Old Testament warns of and the mercy it promises fall on the same afternoon, on the Judge himself. That is stated here as the church's confession. It is not offered as a proof, and it does not explain Jericho.

## What We Did Instead

The church refused Marcion in the second century and has practiced a quieter version of his program in a great many pulpits since. We kept the Old Testament in the binding and stopped reading most of it aloud. We turned the flood into a nursery decoration, with the animals smiling two by two and nobody in the water. We taught children the walls of Jericho as a song about marching. We let congregations assume that the first testament was anger and the second was grace, which is false about both, and when thoughtful people finally read Joshua for themselves they concluded that they had been managed. They had been.

We failed in the opposite direction too, and it was worse. Christians with armies read the wars of Canaan as a permission, cast their own enemies as Canaanites and themselves as Israel, and killed with a clear conscience. The essay on the conquest tells one such story from New England.

## What Stays Hard

The firstborn of the captive in the dungeon is still in the text. So are the infants of Amalek. Each of the readings that faithful Christians give of those passages helps somewhere and costs something, and none makes a parent glad to read them aloud. A reader who finishes the linked pages and is still disturbed has not failed at faith. The Old Testament is full of people who were disturbed by God and said so to his face, and it calls some of them his friends.

What the church decided against Marcion is that the difficulty may not be solved by subtraction. Christians have one God to answer for, and no second, lesser god to whom the hard chapters can be assigned. Marcion offered a Bible with nothing in it to apologize for, and the church chose the longer and harder book, because it believed the God in that book was the one Jesus trusted, and it could not keep Jesus and discard the one he prayed to.

He prayed to that God at the end. Mark records that at the ninth hour he cried out the first line of an Old Testament psalm: "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" (Mark 15:34). He was praying Israel's words to Israel's God, and the prayer was a question. The woman who stopped reading in Joshua has a question of her own, and the church has no answer that makes those chapters easy. What it can tell her is that Jesus read them too, and called their God his Father when he prayed.

*"The Lord, the Lord, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness."* (Exodus 34:6)

*"Whoever has seen me has seen the Father."* (John 14:9)
